title: Electricity from the elements: inorganic electrochemistry, one idea at a time

sections.title: Atoms that give and take electrons
Running it backwards, and other ways to get current

lessons.title: Atoms, electrons and charge
lessons.scope: What electricity is at the atomic scale. Protons and electrons, charge, atomic number; electron shells (2, 8, 8 … simple shell model); valence electrons; the full-shell 'goal'; an atom that loses or gains electrons becomes an ion (cation/anion). Running example: sodium and chlorine. Capstone: build atoms Z = 1–20, strip or add electrons and watch which ions are cheap to make.

lessons.title: The periodic table: who gives, who takes
lessons.scope: The periodic table as a map of electron-giving and electron-taking. Groups and periods; group number ↔ valence electrons; ionisation energy (cost to remove an electron) and its trends; electronegativity (pull on electrons); metals vs non-metals; typical ion charges; why Li, Na, Zn give and O, F, Cl take. Uses Chem.elements data. Capstone: interactive periodic table coloured by trend, 'pick a giver and a taker' experiment.

lessons.title: Ions, salts and electrolytes
lessons.scope: What happens after the electron is given: ionic bonding, charge-balanced formulas (NaCl, MgCl2, Al2O3), polyatomic ions needed later (SO4 2−, OH−, NO3−), crystal lattices; dissolving and dissociation; the mole and molarity (concentration); electrolyte = mobile ions carry current in liquids while electrons carry it in metals. Capstone: conductivity tester, choose a substance and concentration and see the bulb and the ions move.

lessons.title: Oxidation and reduction
lessons.scope: Electron transfer as a reaction. Oxidation = loss, reduction = gain (always paired); half-reactions; oxidation numbers and their rules for inorganic species; oxidising agent and reducing agent. Running example: zinc metal in copper sulfate solution, Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu; spectator ions. Capstone: oxidation-number sandbox, pick a reaction, assign numbers, find who was oxidised and how many electrons moved.

lessons.title: Balancing redox equations
lessons.scope: Electron bookkeeping. Conservation of atoms and of charge; the half-reaction method: split, balance atoms, balance O with H2O and H with H+, balance charge with electrons, scale so electrons cancel, add; converting to basic solution with OH−. Examples: Al + Cu2+, MnO4− + Fe2+ in acid, a reaction in base (Zn + MnO2 alkaline as a preview). Capstone: step-through balancer where the learner sets coefficients and a live atom/charge ledger shows what is still unbalanced.

lessons.title: The activity series: which metal wins
lessons.scope: Which redox reactions actually go. Displacement experiments (metal strips in salt solutions) build a ranking: the activity (reactivity) series; metals above hydrogen dissolve in acid and release H2; spontaneous vs non-spontaneous direction; link back to ionisation energy and why it is not the whole story (hydration of the ion matters: Li). Capstone: virtual lab with 6 metals × 6 salt solutions, the learner runs dips and reconstructs the series.

lessons.title: The galvanic cell: making electrons take the wire
lessons.scope: The central trick of the course. Separate the two half-reactions of Zn + Cu2+ into two beakers so the electrons must travel through a wire: the Daniell cell. Electrode, anode (oxidation) and cathode (reduction); direction of electron flow; why charge builds up and the current stops without a salt bridge or separator; ion flow closes the circuit; cell notation Zn | Zn2+ || Cu2+ | Cu; voltage as push, current as flow (qualitative). Capstone: animated Daniell cell the learner can break (remove bridge, swap metals, short-circuit) and watch electrode masses change.

lessons.title: Electrode potentials: predicting the voltage
lessons.scope: Putting numbers on the activity series. Only differences are measurable, so pick a zero: the standard hydrogen electrode; standard conditions; standard reduction potential E°; the table as a ladder (Chem.E0); E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; positive E°cell = spontaneous; why you do not multiply E° by coefficients; strongest oxidising and reducing agents at the ends (Li, F2). Capstone: cell builder, pick any two half-cells from the table and get voltage, direction of electrons and the overall reaction.

lessons.title: Charge, energy and capacity
lessons.scope: From chemistry to electrical units. Coulomb, ampere = coulomb per second; the Faraday constant (96 485 C per mole of electrons); moles of metal ↔ charge; volt = joule per coulomb, energy = charge × voltage; ΔG = −nFE as 'the chemical energy that came out as electrical work' (Gibbs energy introduced gently as available energy, sign = spontaneity); Ah/mAh and Wh; theoretical specific capacity (mAh/g) = nF/3.6M and why light, multi-electron or low-mass elements (Li, Al, Zn) matter; specific energy Wh/kg. Capstone: 'design a gram' calculator comparing anode elements on capacity and energy.

lessons.title: Concentration and the Nernst equation
lessons.scope: Why a cell's voltage sags as it runs. Non-standard conditions; reaction quotient Q; Le Chatelier intuition (more reactant ion → more push); the Nernst equation E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, 59 mV per decade per electron at 25 °C; concentration cells (same metal, different concentration); a dead cell is at equilibrium: E = 0 ⇔ Q = K, so E° gives K; pH electrode as a one-line application. Capstone: Daniell cell discharge simulator where concentrations drift, voltage follows Nernst and falls to zero at equilibrium.

lessons.title: Zinc: from Volta's pile to the alkaline cell
lessons.scope: The first practical family, all with a zinc anode. Volta's pile and why it faded (hydrogen polarisation); primary vs secondary cells; the zinc–carbon (Leclanché) dry cell: Zn can, MnO2 + carbon cathode, NH4Cl/ZnCl2 paste; the alkaline cell: Zn powder, KOH electrolyte, Zn + 2MnO2 → ZnO + Mn2O3, ~1.5 V, why it outlasts zinc–carbon; zinc–air (oxygen from the air as the cathode reactant, hearing aids); silver oxide button cells in one step. Uses mAh/g from Charge, energy and capacity. Capstone: cutaway AA cell discharge simulator comparing zinc–carbon and alkaline under light and heavy loads.

lessons.title: Lead: the rechargeable car battery
lessons.scope: The first rechargeable battery (Planté, 1859) and still in most cars. One element in three oxidation states: Pb (0), PbSO4 (+2), PbO2 (+4); both electrodes turn into PbSO4 on discharge; sulfuric acid is a reactant, so acid density reveals state of charge; 2.05 V per cell, six in series = 12 V; recharging reverses both half-reactions; overcharge splits water (gassing); sulfation; why it is heavy (Wh/kg) yet delivers huge currents. Capstone: charge/discharge cycle simulator with acid density, voltage and plate composition, including abuse (deep discharge, overcharge).

lessons.title: Nickel: NiCd and NiMH
lessons.scope: Alkaline rechargeables. The nickel oxyhydroxide cathode NiO(OH) ⇌ Ni(OH)2 (Ni +3 ⇌ +2) in KOH, where the electrolyte is not consumed; cadmium anode (NiCd, 1.2 V, toxic, 'memory effect'); replacing Cd with hydrogen stored in a metal alloy (metal hydride, NiMH); nickel–iron (Edison) and nickel–hydrogen (satellites) in brief; flat discharge curve vs alkaline primary; self-discharge. Capstone: compare discharge curves and cycle life of alkaline primary, NiCd and NiMH AA cells in a device simulator.

lessons.title: Lithium: the lightest metal and the ion that shuttles
lessons.scope: Why lithium wins: E° = −3.04 V and 6.94 g/mol (3860 mAh/g); why water is impossible (Li reacts, water splits above ~1.23 V) so inorganic lithium salts (LiPF6) in non-aqueous solvent are used (solvent named only, no organic chemistry); lithium metal primary cells (Li–MnO2 coin cells); dendrites; intercalation: Li+ slides between layers of a host without rebuilding it; graphite anode LiC6 (372 mAh/g), LiCoO2 cathode (Co +3 ⇌ +4), rocking-chair mechanism; cathode families LCO, NMC, LFP (LiFePO4, Fe +2 ⇌ +3), their voltage and trade-offs; the SEI layer in one step. Capstone: rocking-chair simulator, charge and discharge while Li+ moves between hosts and voltage follows the fill level; switch cathode chemistry.

lessons.title: Real batteries: resistance, rate and energy density
lessons.scope: Why real cells deliver less than the thermodynamic numbers. Open-circuit voltage vs voltage under load; internal resistance and V = E − IR, heat = I²R; overpotential in one step (activation, ion transport); C-rate; discharge curves and usable capacity vs rate; power vs energy, the Ragone plot; specific vs volumetric energy; practical Wh/kg of lead–acid, NiMH, Li-ion vs theoretical; series and parallel packs; coulombic and energy efficiency. Capstone: pack designer, choose chemistry, cells in series/parallel and a load and see runtime, sag and heat.

lessons.title: Beyond lithium-ion: sodium, sulfur, solid state and flow
lessons.scope: Other elements competing for the job, judged with the tools already earned (E°, mAh/g, abundance). Sodium-ion (same idea, heavier and bigger ion, cheap and abundant, hard carbon anode named only); lithium–sulfur (S8 + 16Li → 8Li2S, 1672 mAh/g, polysulfide shuttle); lithium metal with solid electrolytes (ceramic/sulfide ion conductors); multivalent ions Mg2+, Al3+ (more electrons per ion, slow in solids); redox flow batteries: all-vanadium, four oxidation states V2+/V3+/VO2+/VO2+ in tanks, energy and power sized separately; liquid-metal and sodium–sulfur high-temperature cells in brief. State of commercialisation dated 'as of 2026'. Capstone: element chooser, pick anode and cathode elements and see theoretical voltage, mAh/g, Wh/kg, crustal abundance and the known catch.
teaches: crustal abundance as a design constraint

lessons.title: Electrolysis: forcing reactions uphill
lessons.scope: Running a cell backwards with an external source. Electrolytic vs galvanic cell (anode is still oxidation, but the signs flip); minimum (decomposition) voltage from E°; Faraday's laws: mass deposited = (I·t / nF)·M; electrolysis of water (2H2O → 2H2 + O2, 1.23 V minimum, 2:1 gas volumes); competing reactions in aqueous salts (why NaCl solution gives H2 and Cl2, not Na): the chlor-alkali process; molten salt electrolysis: sodium (Downs) and aluminium (Hall–Héroult, cryolite, why aluminium is 'solid electricity'); electroplating and copper refining. Capstone: electrolysis bench, pick electrolyte, current and time, predict products and masses, then run.

lessons.title: Hydrogen and fuel cells
lessons.scope: A galvanic cell that is fed instead of discharged. Water electrolysis run in reverse: H2 → 2H+ + 2e−, O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O, 1.23 V ideal; platinum as catalyst (what a catalyst does: lowers the barrier, not the energy), three-phase boundary; PEM (proton-conducting membrane, described by function only), alkaline (Apollo), solid oxide (O2− conducting ceramic, high temperature) variants: which ion crosses; why real cells give ~0.7 V (oxygen reduction is slow, overpotential); efficiency vs a heat engine in one step; hydrogen's energy per kg vs per litre; the electrolyser + fuel cell round trip. Capstone: polarisation-curve simulator, draw more current and watch voltage, power and efficiency; stack cells to hit a target power.

lessons.title: Corrosion: the battery you did not want
lessons.scope: Rust as a short-circuited galvanic cell. Anodic and cathodic sites on one piece of iron; Fe → Fe2+ + 2e−, O2 + 2H2O + 4e− → 4OH−, then Fe(OH)2 → rust (Fe2O3·xH2O); why water, oxygen and salt all matter (electrolyte!); galvanic corrosion between two touching metals (use the potential ladder); protection: paint, sacrificial anode (zinc, magnesium), galvanising, impressed current (cathodic protection), passivation: why aluminium, chromium (stainless steel) and titanium survive despite negative E°; a lemon/seawater battery as the same chemistry turned useful. Capstone: 'protect the ship hull' simulator, choose metals in contact, the environment and a protection method and watch which metal dissolves and how fast.

lessons.title: Silicon and light: electricity without a reaction
lessons.scope: The other great way elements produce electricity: no redox, light moves the electrons. Silicon's four valence electrons and the covalent crystal (shared pairs, introduced here); why pure silicon barely conducts; band gap as the energy to free a bonded electron (1.1 eV; eV introduced from volt × electron charge); electron and hole; doping with group 15 phosphorus (n-type) and group 13 boron (p-type); the p–n junction and its built-in field; a photon with enough energy makes an electron–hole pair and the junction separates it: photovoltaic effect; why one cell gives ~0.6 V; photons below the gap are lost and the excess above it becomes heat (efficiency limit, stated not derived); other element choices (GaAs, CdTe) in brief; contrast with a battery: no stored charge, a converter. Capstone: solar cell simulator, set light intensity, band gap and load and trace the I–V curve to the maximum power point.
teaches: I–V curve and maximum power point
